source.title: Retrieving Convex Bodies from Restricted Covariogram Functions

accepted.question_text: For a planar convex body K in two-dimensional Euclidean space, define its covariogram by g_K(x) = area(K intersect (K + x)). Since translating K or reflecting K in a point leaves this function unchanged, does g_K determine K among all planar convex bodies up to translations and point reflections? Equivalently, if X and Y are independent random variables uniformly distributed over K, does the distribution of X - Y determine K up to translations and point reflections?

evidence.quote: Let K be a convex body in E d . The covariogram gK of K is the function gK(x) = V (K ∩ (K + x)), where x ∈ E d and V denotes volume in E d .

The covariogram gK is clearly unchanged by a translation or a reflection of K. (The term reflection will always means reflection in a point.) Matheron [Mat86] and, independently, Adler and Pyke [AP97] asked the following question. Covariogram problem. Does the covariogram determine a convex body, among all convex bodies, up to translations and reflections?
Matheron conjectured a positive answer for the case d = 2, but this conjecture has not been completely settled.

Adler and Pyke [AP91, AP97] asked Matheron’s question in probabilistic terms. Does the distribution of the difference X − Y of independent random variables X and Y uniformly distributed over K determine K, up to translations and reflections? Since the convolution in (1) is, up to a multiplicative factor, the probability density of X − Y , this problem is equivalent to the covariogram one.

accepted.question_text: Let K and H be planar convex bodies. Let g_K be the covariogram of K, let D_K = {x - y : x and y are in K} be the difference body of K, let bd D_K be its boundary, and let o be the origin. For a closed set X, say GC(X) holds when g_K(x) = g_H(x) for all x in some neighborhood of X. Suppose K is strictly convex and has no local symmetry, where a local symmetry is a pair of closed boundary arcs of K that are reflections of each other in a point, have disjoint nonempty relative interiors, and are not properly contained in a larger pair with the same properties. If X is either {o} or bd D_K and GC(X) holds, must K and H coincide up to translations and point reflections, even when K is not assumed to have a twice continuously differentiable boundary with all principal curvatures nonzero?
accepted.context_brief: Strictly convex globally non-symmetric planar bodies

evidence.quote: GC(X) The equality gK(x) = gH(x) holds for all x in some neighbourhood of X.

A pair of closed boundary arcs of a planar convex body K is said to be a local symmetry of K if they are reflections of each other in a point, have disjoint and nonempty relative interiors, and they are not properly contained in a pair of boundary arcs with the same properties. A planar convex body K is called locally symmetric if it possesses a local symmetry. Planar convex bodies without local symmetries are called globally non-symmetric.
It is known that the support of gK is the difference body of K, DK = {x − y : x, y ∈ K}, and that DK is o-symmetric.
II. If K is globally non-symmetric and X is either {o} or bd DK, then GC(X) implies the coincidence of K and H, up to translations and reflections.

It is an open question whether Part II of the above theorem holds for all strictly convex K not necessarily C 2 + . The positive answer to this question would imply the confirmation of Matheron’s conjecture for all planar convex bodies.

accepted.question_text: Let K and H be convex bodies in d-dimensional Euclidean space with d >= 3. Let g_K be the covariogram of K, let D_K = K + (-K) be the difference body of K, and let bd D_K be its boundary. Say GC(bd D_K) holds when g_K(x) = g_H(x) for all x in some neighborhood of bd D_K. Suppose K is C^2_+, meaning its boundary is a twice continuously differentiable manifold and all principal curvatures are nonzero. Does GC(bd D_K) imply local coincidence LC, meaning that for every boundary point p of K there is a boundary point q of H and some epsilon > 0 such that K intersect (p + epsilon B^d) and H intersect (q + epsilon B^d) coincide up to translations and point reflections, and the same condition also holds with K and H interchanged?
accepted.context_brief: Higher-dimensional boundary covariogram versus local coincidence

evidence.quote: GC(X) The equality gK(x) = gH(x) holds for all x in some neighbourhood of X.

A convex body K is said to belong to the class C 2 + if its boundary is a two-times continuously differentiable manifold and all its principal curvatures are non-zero (for detailed information see [Sch93b, Section 2.5]).

LC For every boundary point p of K there exists a boundary point q of H such that for some ε > 0 the bodies K∩(p+εB d ) and H∩(q+εB d ) coincide, up to translations and reflections; the same statement also holds with the roles of K and H interchanged.
It is an open problem whether for C 2 + convex bodies in E d , d ≥ 3, the condition GC(bd DK) implies LC.

accepted.question_text: In d-dimensional Euclidean space with d >= 3, consider convex bodies K and H and the covariograms g_K and g_H. Say GC({o}) holds when g_K(x) = g_H(x) for all x in some neighborhood of the origin o. In the Baire category sense, where a property holds for most convex bodies if the exceptions form at most a meager set and a meager set is a countable union of nowhere dense sets, is it true that for most convex bodies K, every convex body H satisfying GC({o}) must coincide with K up to translations and point reflections?
accepted.context_brief: Baire-generic origin covariogram data in higher dimensions

evidence.quote: GC(X) The equality gK(x) = gH(x) holds for all x in some neighbourhood of X.

Thus, we may speak about statements that hold for most convex bodies, i.e., for all convex bodies with at most a meager set of exceptions. We recall that a set is said to be meager if it is a countable union of nowhere dense sets and residual if it is a complement of a meager set.
Theorem 6. In the Baire category sense, for most convex bodies K and all convex bodies H in E d the following statements hold true.
II. If d = 2 and K and H satisfy GC({o}), then K and H coincide, up to translations and reflections.
It is an open question whether Part II of the statement can be carried over to convex bodies of higher dimensions.

accepted.question_text: For a convex body, does the distribution of the lengths of its chords, taken in all directions, characterize the body up to rigid motions?

evidence.quote: Blaschke (cf. [San04]) asked whether the distribution of the lengths of chords (in all directions) of a convex body characterizes the body, up to rigid motions, but Mallows and Clark [MC70] proved that this is false even for convex polygons.
